utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before entering the courtroom, I was told by the Registrar that today marks the 300th trial day. Well, before we begin today the Chamber would like to deal with one pending matter. On the 11th of October, 2012, the Registrar issued a decision on the accused's indigency in which he determined that the accused should financially contribute to his own defence. On the 15th of October, 2012, the accused filed a request for an extension of time, namely, until 26th of November, 2012, in which to file an application for a review of the Registrar's decision. In support of this request, the accused argues that the extension is needed because the issues involved in the review are complex, his defence case has commenced, and he is presently litigating a number of issues before the Appeals Chamber. The accused also seeks access to a confidential and ex parte decision from another case because it is referred to in footnotes 40 and 58 of the confidential and ex parte appendix 2 to the Registrar's decision. The Chamber notes that in footnote 40 of that appendix, the Registrar expresses willingness to disclose the said decision if ordered to do so by the Chamber. The Chamber also notes that on the 15th of October, 2012, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the accused via e-mail that it did not intend to file a response to the accused's request. Having considered the accused's request, the Chamber has decided to grant the extension of time sought; thus the accused shall file his application for a review of the Registrar's decision by no later than 26th November 2012. The Chamber also orders the Registry to provide the accused with the confidential and ex parte decision referred to in footnotes 40 and 58 of the confidential and ex parte appendix 2 to the Registrar's decision. Further, there is one matter I would like to clarify with the accused in relation to the associated exhibit with Mr. Kovacevic's evidence. One of the items was noted as 1D2337 in his notification, but, actually, if we look at the paragraph 49 of the Statute [sic] it refers to 1D8452. But the trouble is that the 1D8452 does not appear on e-court, and I'm not sure the correct document may be 1D2337. So in the meantime if the Defence could check it out. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Oh, I'm sorry, I forgot to give the witness a warning we discussed. General Kovacevic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Yugoslav Tribunal. Under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. General, do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you heard the translation? Has the microphone been activated? Yes, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Listening to Dr. Karadzic read a summary of your evidence yesterday, I was struck by a couple of things I wanted to clear up with you, kind of preliminary things, before we begin, if that's okay. First, when you met with me a couple of days ago - and thank you for that - you clarified your present occupation and said that you were actually at this time working with the Federal Ministry of Defence as an advisor in education and training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How does that make you an active officer within the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the personnel of the armed forces are also employees of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your rank is actually brigadier, not brigadier-general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that I was a brigadier. That is actually the highest rank for the officers that we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And also in reading out a summary of your evidence, Dr. Karadzic said this, he said: "Passage of humanitarian convoys was completely unhindered by Serb forces." And then I looked at paragraph 39 of your statement, I saw that you really hadn't said that but what you said on the subject of humanitarian aid was pretty specific. So just to avoid any wrong impressions, I thought I would read to you what you said at paragraph 39. You said: "At Grbavica there was a passage through which humanitarian relief convoys passed, and I know that Adra, which was a Muslim humanitarian organisation, and Caritas, which was a Croatian organisation crossed over to the other side of town unhindered via the bridge near the school of economics." So you were actually referring to passage at a specific location of two specific charities into Grbavica and nothing wider than that; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just one more sort of preliminary thing. The summary of your evidence referred to something called the 110th Brigade of the ABiH 1st Corps, which you said in your statement at paragraph 18 was commanded by Dusan Topalovic. But given your position at the time of the conflict and what you said you knew about Muslim units in Sarajevo, you must have known that there was never actually any 110th Brigade in Sarajevo and Topalovic's brigade was called the 10th Mountain Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the designation of the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Dusan Topalovic was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think the interpreters didn't hear the first part of what you said about the unit, the designation of the unit. Could you just repeat that for them.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been a mistake in the transcript. The 1st Corps, the 1st Brigade, was 1.0, which means 10, the 10th Mountain Brigade. I know that for a fact and I know that Dusan Topalovic, Caco, was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That was just to clarify the designation of the brigade as it appeared in your statement. And Topalovic was killed and his unit was eliminated in October 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was not eliminated. The unit was reformed, reorganised in a way. However, in its essence it remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was Topalovic killed in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I learned that from the media. I can't claim that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to focus on your time in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade for a while, you said you were chief of operations and training in that brigade. What does that mean? What was your job there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time my job was to organise the training of the units of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does the chief of operations do?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade does not have the chief of operations. Operations and training are one and the same; they are unified.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who planned operations within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade staff plans operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I remember you told me a couple of days ago that you were number three in the brigade. Does that mean that you were part of the brigade staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a staff member.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were involved in the planning of brigade operations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to move on to some of the areas of tactical responsibility of your brigade, I'd just like to give you a couple of landmark locations and have you confirm whether or not those were within your brigade's area of responsibility. And the first location I'd like to ask you about is the Orthodox church at Veljine. Was that within the area of tactical responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the term Veljine. Do you mean Veljine church? It was in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the -- that's the church I mean. Thank you. How about the Slavisa Vajner-Cica barracks at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The length of Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ozrenska, Ulica is much longer. So one part of the street was under the control of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, but the other part wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about the skyscrapers at what's now Grbavicka Street, that would be skyscrapers in particular at number 6, 6A, and number 8.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with their numbers, the numbers of the skyscrapers, but I'm familiar with the names of the streets. One was Milutina Djuraskovica Street and there was a skyscraper there on the left-hand side and it was in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I can show you a picture because it's easier sometimes to see pictures. We don't know the addresses always of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 23858, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These skyscrapers, Brigadier, were they in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this on the left bank of the Miljacka river?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on the south bank of the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My zone of responsibility was not there so I don't know whether those facilities were occupied were not. They could have also been some sort of interspace between various units.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These are within your brigade, Brigadier, and these are the skyscrapers at Grbavicka 6 , 6A, 8, and 8A. Were they in your brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, yes, they were. If they are on the left bank of the Miljacka river, then, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We don't need that picture anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Vrace monument, was that in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Osmice?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring only to the bed and breakfast facility Osmice, then yes, but not the entire Osmice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The bed and breakfast facility, yes, thank you. Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatiste is also a feature which also featured a tower. The tower was in our hands, under our control, but Zlatiste as an area was not, not an entire area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how far east did your brigade's area of responsibility go?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to talk about the area of responsibility. It is, indeed, a military term; however, our units were undermanned so in effect they had no depth. So instead of talking about zones of responsibility, you should rather talk about front lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask to clarify something in the transcript. In the transcript it says that "they didn't go in-depth," whereas the general, or rather, the brigadier said that they did not have the necessary depth and I think that there is a major difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be clarified by the CLSS later on. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Taking onboard your comment, can you tell me how far to the east the area or zone or line held by your brigade extended?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The average depth of defence for the brigade was conditional upon the deployment of the units in the zone. The command post and the artillery positions were in-depth, about 2 to 3 kilometres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I keep asking you about east and you keep telling me about depth. I wonder if we have a problem understanding one another?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking from the point of view, the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was eastwards from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did it go as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Brigadier Kovacevic said that it didn't occupy the area east of Sarajevo. I believe that his answer was negative rather than positive, and that may have an impact on the further course of Madam Edgerton's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall I ask the witness to repeat his answer? Yes, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Sarajevo Brigade did not have a front line facing Sarajevo from the east. It was rather from the south. That was part of the front line. The front line, however, was fragmented, so you cannot really say that it was in the east or in the west. It would be impossible to state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just leave that and come back to that later. Thank you. Brigadier, your brigade, let's talk more about your brigade and its units and its battalions, your brigade had among its battalions a mixed artillery battalion and an anti-aircraft battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was the command post of the mixed artillery battalion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Tilava. And to be more precise, it was in Uzdojnice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were those the firing points or the firing positions of that battalion or were there additional positions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was there, the basic positions, the reserve positions. In other words, the unit spent the entire war there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what heavy weapons did it have at those locations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "heavy weapons"? It was a standard type of unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I was to be more precise perhaps I could say: What heavy weapons of 120 millimetres and above did it have at those locations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it had a 122-millimetre howitzer battery, 155-millimetre battery, and VBR Plamen battery 128-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How many weapons form a battery?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, between four to eight pieces, but not necessarily. Depends largely on any given situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's a Plamen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the small multi-rocket launcher used for closer-range fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were there any 120-millimetre mortars also located with the mixed artillery battalion at these locations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a mixed artillery battalion there were no 120-millimetre mortars. However, I know that there was an agreement on the concentration and control of weapons, and according to that agreement that type of weaponry was transferred from all infantry battalions to that particular battalion. All that time at the command post of that battalion there was an observer mission of the United Nations. I remember Sanja Zverovic [phoen] who was their permanent interpreter. The rest of the staff changed. I must also add to this that due to frequent incidents in Sarajevo very often it was insisted upon UNPROFOR to confirm whether fire was opened or whether it wasn't opened. The log-book that was kept at that command post would be very good material for this type of exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll come back to this in more detail, but when you just referred to a log-book do you mean an artillery log-book?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each unit keeps its own record. Here I was referring to the log-book kept by UNPROFOR observers in which they recorded each and every fire opened from any point and from any zone where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, but I was referring to an artillery log-book. Did the brigade, since you know what kind of log-books seem to be kept there, did the brigade keep an artillery log-book that noted each and every fire from every point and what the results of that engagement of fire might have been?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade keeps a field diary and it records the operations of all units, not only artillery. And the results achieved can only be assumed. You cannot enter into a log-book the impact of a specific projectile. The people simply wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll leave that for the moment and just continue on with the battalions in your brigade. You confirmed you had an anti-aircraft battalion, and where was that located? Where was its command post?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PVO battalion was practically pointless because in 1992 or July of 1992, due to the hand-over of the airport to the United Nations, in the area of the Sarajevo airport all PVO pieces of weaponry were withdrawn by us from the area around the airport. To all intents and purposes there was no effectively functional PVO artillery in Sarajevo, only some of the 20-millimetre guns or 30-millimetre guns served as anti-infantry weapons because it is possible to use them for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thanks for that answer, but I actually asked you something completely different and that was where the headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms it did not operate at all. It was attached to the artillery unit. It existed there as a matter of formality, but it was not there practically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the 20- and 30-millimetre guns that were used as anti-infantry weapons, where were they then deployed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were deployed on the outer ring, as we used to call it, around Sarajevo towards Trnovo, then some of them were in Praca towards Gorazde. Some of them were in Nisici, conditionally speaking, facing Olovo. So these artillery pieces could be more effective in an open area rather than in urban areas. They cannot be used in urban areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So they were within the battalions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were given to infantry battalions, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also had a tank battalion within the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an armoured battalion in the brigade. It was deployed, or rather, one company was deployed at the old airport called Butmir, where now is situated the base of the European forces in Sarajevo. Another company was in Jahorinski Potok at Pale a little bit further from Pale towards Praca. And there was another company in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how many tanks did the armoured battalion have?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, three or four and 27 tanks, but in this specific instance that was not the case, there were fewer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind were they, T55s? T34s?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the tanks were T55.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I want to go on to another topic now and it's the topic of snipers, because in your statement you said, "There were no trained professional snipers in my unit." And I'm actually not sure what we're supposed to understand for that. And you use the word "unit" a lot in your statement, so sometimes we can only guess what you're referring to. So here when you said that, did you mean to refer to your brigade or your battalion or something else?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke in my statement, you can make a clear distinction in terms of what the unit was at the time when I was the chief of the operations and training department in the brigade. I was describing the situation and what I was doing there at the time. When I was the battalion commander I described the situation pertaining to that position, so I don't know what is it you don't understand so please can you be more specific in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. When you said there were no trained professional snipers in my unit, were you referring to the battalion or the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the passage to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. So it's paragraph 36 of P2331. And of course he'd need to see the version in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you read out the passage para 36 or -- yes, para 36 and for the benefit of the witness could you kindly read out that passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brigadier, in paragraph 36 you said: "There were no trained professional snipers in my unit. The story about snipers in Sarajevo is unnecessary, if one knows and takes into account the fact that snipers fire at salient targets at greater distances. At all positions in Sarajevo, and in particular my unit, fire could be opened by weapons of any type including shot-guns because the distances are very small. I had information that there existed snipers in the units of the 1st ABH Corps ranged against us." So by "unit" here, are you referring to the brigade or the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I was referring to the battalion because I spoke from that position, but I can also tell you what is the case with the brigade because I am familiar with that too since I was the person in charge of training units. I had never organised nor conducted any training of snipers. Snipers in units are selected on the basis of their physical and psychological features and traits, based on their inclinations, and they are subjected to special shooting training. They are giving a special VES, which is a military specialty recorded in their military card, and I can categorically assert that in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade there were no such personnel. When I said that it was unnecessary, you can see in the maps that you have shown me that the separation lines were 20 to 50 metres on the average. Any person who knows anything about weapons will understand that optical devices cannot be used at these ranges. That all small infantry weapons can be used in such situations, that is true, and that from the military point of view setting up sniper fire is completed pointless.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when we talk about, for example, the group of snipers that were commanded by Nebojsa Ivkovic who operated in the area of the 2nd Battalion, who are we talking about then? Are we talking about specially trained snipers or are we talking about pretty good sharpshooters who could fire at targets with small infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance with the interpretation? Sharpshooters are those who fire; that's how it's translated in our language. And that's not what the witness received in terms of translation because this specific term is very rarely used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question because of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. In these buildings that we showed you the picture of earlier on at Grbavicka Street, for example, there was a sniper unit that was operational commanded by Nebojsa Ivkovic and others. Now -- so when we talk about that unit what type of shooter are we talking about, a sniper or sharpshooters firing at targets with small infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nebojsa Ivkovic was never in the 3rd Infantry Battalion, never. I heard of this man towards the end of the war. I saw him at Grbavica and I also don't think that he had any role in the 2nd Battalion either but I'm not sure of that. I have to tell you that the 1st Sarajevo Brigade had never issued such order because otherwise I as the commander of the battalion would have received it. There were individuals, however, who wanted to portray themselves as being some sort of specialists in order to boost their image. I suppose that's how he represented himself, but I don't know that in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade there was no organised sniper group, and, frankly speaking, I don't know what the purpose would be of such a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you disputing that the brigade had firing positions in the buildings on Grbavicka Street?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing that they had firing positions. However, I dispute that they had sniper groups; that was not the case. The brigade did not organise such things. I know that for sure and I'm positive, otherwise I would have received an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For people in these firing positions, were they equipped with any special arms that would help them carry out their mission?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure exactly what kind of weapons were issued to 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Not a single piece out of establishment or beyond establishment was issued to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what we're supposed to understand when you say "establishment," establishment weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably you had an opportunity to see how the units are formed. It is very exactly specified, the manpower, the weaponry, and how units are formed. Brigades are not group kind of motley crew in which everyone does whatever they please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we can try again and I can help you with this by showing you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we see 65 ter 23823, please. And we should have it available in translation and the original language. It's dated -- it's from Veljko Stojanovic, commander of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, dated 29 October 1993 to General Galic. I think you need to collapse the text on the right-hand side of the page and give us the original document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, this document is issued by your brigade's commander, Stojanovic, responding to General Galic's order and informing General Galic that the brigade possesses four M48 7.9-millimetre rifles with optical sights; two 7.62-millimetre semi-automatic rifles with optical sights; three M48 7.62-millimetre machine-guns with optical sights; 12, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifles; ten M76 7.9-millimetre sniper rifles; two 7.62-millimetre rifles with passive infrared sights; four silencers; and four 7.62-millimetre rifle silencers. And Colonel Stojanovic says within your brigade they had no separate sniper unit but had sniper guns among soldiers within the brigades and they were active when they were at the front lines. So are these establishment weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo Corps and the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade didn't have units only facing the city. Only a few units were deployed there. The majority of units were deployed in the manoeuvre area towards the outer ring. And this is where this type of weapons is prominent and it is only natural for the commander to know whether all these weapons were provided. So there is nothing special about it. There was nothing extraordinary that was not regularly brought to these units. The Croatian and the Muslim forces had identical weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying that brigade units at the confrontation line in Sarajevo did not possess any of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. An optical sight can be mounted on any kind of rifle, including hunting rifles. But each person having this kind of weapons does not mean that this person is a sniper. In that case you can say that all hunters are snipers if you apply that logic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just talking about units deployed on the inner ring - just talking about that for a moment - who used these weapons, what would their mission be?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago at distances where the front part of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was deployed in populated areas, these are places where due to the closeness of the ranges it was impossible to use optical devices. I cannot explain maybe to the detail to you what urban operations mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Units, the inner ring who used these weapons, who planned their fire?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be no planning on fire. A soldier is either in a trench or within a facility. He's observing the area in front of him and whatever appears there that poses a danger he will open fire; if there's no danger, there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of reporting did these units have to make? Did they have to report every kill?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who fires a shot, he doesn't know whether he made a kill or not. So how can he send a report to that effect? This is beyond comprehension.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying that a person firing a rifle shot wouldn't see target impact? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that you don't understand me because you were not in this position. A soldier on the line makes his own decision whether he will shoot or not based on the risk assessment that he himself makes. If he were really in danger and if he waited to send a report and then wait for an order to open fire, he would have been killed a hundred times in the meantime. So that is completely pointless and senseless. Generally speaking, when the chain of command is set up, an order is issued what kind of regime fire is going to be applied. And most often amongst our ranks we had to wait because we were forced to prove that we were not the ones who opened fire first but rather did it in self-defence. Unfortunately, due to that we suffered losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go on to -- thank you for that. Let's go on to one other unit within your battalion. In your statement at paragraph 43 you talked about volunteers in the ranks of your unit and by that - and since we're talking about your battalion - are you -- do you mean to refer to Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not referring to him alone. He was one of the volunteers. Actually, he was not a volunteer, he was the man who lived at the Jewish cemetery and he felt the need to portray himself as a Chetnik which was basically contrary to what he was actually doing because he had been mobilised, just like everybody else, in a regular procedure, and he was in that position. I don’t think that his political orientation as a radical should be linked to what he was doing. It has nothing to do with it. Slavko Aleksic was not a member of the paramilitary. You can check this and find evidence of it because, just like all the others, it can be found in the basic VOB8 book, including all the members of his unit. It was no paramilitary. They were people who for political reasons portrayed themselves as Chetniks and radicals but were local people. There were volunteers from other countries among them as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript again. It should say he represented himself as a Chetnik and a radical, not Chetnik and volunteer. And earlier the witness said he had not been a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That’s right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Aleksic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness confirmed what I said but it's not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, the -- CLSS will sort it out later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did Aleksic's unit have mortars?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of fire-arms did they have?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Infantry weapons without any large calibres, nothing larger than a light machine-gun or a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did they have sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like all other units. That was called anti-armoured company. They had hand-held launchers for anti-armour combatted and they had only rifles within that unit, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were their mission?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their exclusive and standing mission was not to allow passage through the Jewish cemetery, and their defence line was the entry into the Bosut barracks, which is on the edge of the Jewish cemetery, until the roundabout road in Sarajevo. That's where they started the war and where they finished it, at the wall of the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who provided equipment and materiel to Aleksic's unit? How did they get their supplies?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksic got weapons just like all other units. His was a regular unit within the battalion and within the brigade. It was a regular supply. This was not a paramilitary unit. In his unit, apart from local residents of the local commune of Kovacici, practically the Jewish cemetery, there were also a few volunteers. Maybe that's the element that introduces the confusion, but all units are supplied in the regular way, including his.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does "the regular way" mean through the battalion command and then to the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to another document, but before I do that, Your Honours, could I ask that the last one 65 ter 23823 be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look now at 65 ter 23874. It's a request from Slavko Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, on the screen in front of you is a document from Slavko Aleksic's anti-tank company dated September 16, 1993, to you personally, asking for, among other things, 7.62 automatic rifles; ten crates; 7.62 Brownings; incendiary bullets; a 7.9 sniper rifle; an 82-millimetre mortar; slow-burning fuses; TNT, and so forth. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So why did you say Aleksic's unit had no mortars?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's requesting them. He didn't have a mortar. That doesn't mean that the request was approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, it's directed to you. Did you approve it or not?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, I had a constant problem because they were not a permanent unit, not a permanent force. They were just mobilised and their military knowledge was not very good. These people were megalomaniacs. They were afraid. They wanted to have all sorts of things in reserve. But I was a man who knew these things and I never approved this. And this went on all the time. I never approved any of this. They asked for planes. This is a regular thing. None of this was approved because I couldn't approve that they get something that I didn't have. I told you a moment ago that the supply to our units was very professional in the way it was done and it's in all our reports. It's standard practice. Nobody could by-pass the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you expect us to take seriously that they asked for airplanes?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is they also wanted air support. I'm telling you this seriously. He's thinking: We'll be captured, killed. They panic. And of course sometimes they were in danger but not that kind. You have no idea about this, but I've lived through a lot of things. These were not professionally trained troops for warfare. These were local residents who were fearful. The basic issue is: Who will help me on the line when I am in danger? And I give them everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you also said in that same paragraph that these volunteers --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again there is an error in the transcript. The witness didn't say "I provided it all." It was their question and indeed the interpreter didn't understand this because it was not clear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But Mr. Karadzic is saying the witness said actually they said in their requests: Give us everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a phonetic mark there which will be clarified by the court reporters later on. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have this document 65 ter 23874 as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to go on to another topic and it's about something you said at paragraph 24 of your statement. You said: "It was only in the Muslim mass media that I saw that the possible victims of combat between our units and adversary units of the 1st BiH army corps had been civilians. On our side we had such cases, notably on 6 January 1994 when the Muslims executed an attack on the Jewish cemetery and the Vrbanja bridge." So just one more clarification, these civilian victims you're mentioning here in this paragraph, you mean to refer to victims in Bosnian-held territory; right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the first part when I said that I got information from the media about losses on the Muslim side - and I'm saying the same thing now - I didn't know what was going on in Sarajevo and whether it was really so. I watched that on television. But since I know how a media war is conducted - and this time the enemy side did not hide it, they openly announced it - I knew that many incidents were rigged but that was all I knew. I didn't know anything else. The only other way was to find out from people who crossed over to our side from defectors and they would tell us what had happened there. How truthful that was only they know; I myself wasn't there. And this case on the 6th of June [as interpreted], 1994, that I mentioned on our side was just to illustrate. Whenever there are combat operations in a populated area, considering that the civilians lived practically along the lines, not far behind the lines, civilians suffer much more than troops. Civilians find it harder to get under cover and they suffer disproportionally. That was just one case and there were many of them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually just want to make a transcript correction or a clarification. You referred to a case on 6 June 1994. Did you mean to refer to the case on 6 January 1994 that you mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: January.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you just said you didn't know what was going on in Sarajevo and whether it was really so. And I wonder if by saying that, do you mean to say that you had no forward observation of anything that was going on in the city?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, an urban area, that is impossible. There is no room to organise any such thing ahead of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you had no forward observation of any targets you might be seeking to engage?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what can be seen from the line at a distance of 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Brigadier, you've said in your statement that you took measures to avoid collateral damage when determining whether or not to engage a target. How does -- how can you say you do that when you have no forward observation of your targets?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply. My unit which is in contact cannot put anything ahead of them, nothing forward, because 20 metres ahead they would be already in Muslim territory. That's impossible. Considering that it's a city, you see the street, you cannot see through buildings. A rifle cannot shoot through a building. It can shoot through passages, along the street, and that's it. A hand-grenade can be thrown outside a building. You can set a mine in front of a trench, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you fired your weapons with no forward observation, I'm actually really curious about what measures you did take to avoid collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking an impossible answer. The separation line, I repeat, is on average 20 to 50 metres. The interval, the space in between in urban areas are houses. You cannot see through houses. You can only see through streets leading to some area. You can only see if one house is much taller than the others, but not far ahead. And to claim that somebody could see from Grbavica what was going on in Bascarsija, that person is crazy; or even 100 metres ahead across the Miljacka river, that's impossible. It can't be seen. You can't see that sort of thing in a city. Get out of this building into the street and look around, you can only see the street. You can't see behind the next building. And what need is there to guide infantry shooters? They can see for themselves. Not every bullet hits the target. There are also ricochets, there are misses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually think I'm not asking for an impossible answer because you said in your statement at paragraph 32, and I'll read it to you: "When executing combat actions and opening fire at military targets located at civilian zones, we took measures to reduce collateral civilian damage." And then you gave one example, one example. So I'm actually asking you for some other examples.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply - and that's true - the order not to open fire without need avoids unnecessary casualties, that's one; two, to shoot at a target which is a threat, not to shoot any-old-how, that's another measure; refraining from senselessly open fire when there is no reason. Those are the measures. Those are simple things, nothing spectacular, nothing special. Those are normal things. We were not philosophers there to create some odd conditions. Those are the things you are able to do in a situation like that. It's more like appealing to the conscience of the soldier in the trench, to be composed, to be smart, to protect himself without endangering unnecessarily others.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can we understand from that that it was up to the soldier himself to judge the threat and whatever danger he might be facing in determining whether he was going to respond and how he was going to respond? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. The soldier in the trench, if he were to wait for somebody else to make the decision whether he's going to defend himself or not would have never been able to defend himself. It is natural that the enemy will catch you out in any moment of inattention to incur losses, to inflict losses. Everything else is a lie and an illusion. Nobody else but the person in the trench who is in danger has to make that decision. But he doesn't decide whether there will be combat or not. That's why there is a command. He only decides about himself. The squad commander decides about the squad, the platoon commander decides about the platoon, and so on. That's why we have hierarchy. That's why we have organisation. We must admit that this works better where we have professional trained units. Where the men are not so well trained, it works less well, there are more mistakes, and we can talk about the quality of units. That's what makes a difference between them, whether they're trained or not, whether the personnel in the trenches is able as a unit or as a group to execute a mission or not. That's how we have to evaluate them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about -- you talked about the soldier in the trench. How about the soldier who fires the 60- or 82-millimetre mortar, is it up to him to decide when he should fire and what might be the appropriate response to the threat?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the same thing. A mortar is a collective weapon. In the army there are weapons handled by individuals and weapons operated by crews including artillery weapons. Artillery weapons cannot be used without the order of the commander, such are mortars and artillery weapons. That's how they are different from a personal weapon. A personal weapon is issued to a soldier and he decides on how to use it. Collective weapons are issued to a unit and the commander decides how they are used. An individual cannot decide without the commander how to use a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- but in your statement at paragraphs 23 and 28 you said, effectively, it had been ordered from the SRK command that fire was to be opened only if lives were directly threatened. So did that apply only to the soldier in the trenches or the soldier with the infantry weapon, or did it also apply to the soldiers handling the mortars?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a corps commander issues such an order - because you mentioned the corps commander - then he obviously has information that it is a larger operation and the area of responsibility of the corps is under threat; then all resources are put into operation. Any commander who makes the decision probably has information about what's going on ahead of him, so all people are put at readiness. But placing them at readiness does not mean that they go into action. Action starts only when the order comes from the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll read to you what you said in paragraph 23. You said: "It had been ordered many times from all SRK command levels that fire was to be opened only if lives were directly threatened and then only at targets endangering the security of the unit." So then if I was to read that I would think that whoever fired the weapon was left to decide when they should fire and what might be the appropriate response; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about placing a unit at readiness in expectation of some action. They are placed at readiness. I said a moment ago, a soldier looks around him. It's a narrow belt, 20 to 50 metres, not more, as far as a soldier can see and he doesn't have to see much farther. And in that narrow area he will certainly be able to make a decision if he is in danger. He will report if he has time; if he doesn't have time to report, he will of course defend himself. But collective weapons act only upon an observed target upon orders. If that soldier in the trench sees a group ahead of him, he reports it and then the command decides how to take action, whether to open fire, and how to open fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you've just said, and I've pressed you on that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your statement you said at paragraph 44: "It was frequently the case that fire would be opened from mobile mortars located near civilian buildings like the hospital compound, the Presidency, and the TV building to provoke a reaction from the Serbian side." About these mobile mortars, what routinely were the size of those mortars?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the school centre Marsal Tito before the war. In the school centre Marsal Tito there were collective weapons for the training of recruits, among them a large number of 60-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetres, and 120-millimetres. There were also other weapons, tanks, T55 armoured personnel carriers, recoilless guns and other guns --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brigadier, Brigadier, I asked you about the size of the mobile mortars you spoke about in paragraph 44. I didn't ask you anything about the Marsal Tito stocks.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the assets were taken from the Marsal Tito and mounted on trucks. On each truck you can place a platform for a mortar that can then fire successfully. You fire one or two shells and then the truck moves. Those are the tactics of creating an image that there is a large number of mortars, sowing panic and confusion. But most often fire is opened suddenly and the first projectiles kill the most people before the others flee. Since in Sarajevo, especially in the neighbourhood of Grbavica, there was a tunnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, that was a sufficient answer. She asked about the size of the mobile mortar. Shall we take a break now, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much long longer would you need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No more than one session and possibly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brigadier, we left on the subject of mobile mortars and I just want to stay with that subject for a little while more because in your evidence today you said that collective weapons acted only on an observed target or orders. So from this can we take that any response to a report that a mobile mortar had fired would be ordered by a command level?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the fire opened on such targets, there has to be information as to where from such fire was opened. Secondly, there were duty crews on the weaponry in all of our units and they could easily observe. If fire was not returned immediately, then any further attempt to that effect became pointless because the target, being a mobile mortar, the main objective was to damage such a target, move the area -- move from the area rapidly, and provoke the enemy's side response. Things were done so that fire was opened and targeted the area in front of such facilities that had to be protected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. From line 17 onwards the message of the witness's answer has not been conveyed properly. Line 17 [In English] "... the target, being a mobile ..." [Interpretation] It was not target but [In English] mobile mortar to damage the other side and the sense to respond was while it was there. So, please, from 17 to 21. It is not catched what the witness meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's difficult to follow what you said at the moment and it's also distracting. If you have some translation issue, you could intervene later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meaning is completely lost, the entire passage consisting of four or five lines. And as we read the transcript the meaning of the witness's answer is completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of me intervening, could you repeat your question, having heard Mr. Karadzic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could try it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you or your superiors sign-off on the engagement of every response to mobile mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't respond by signing anything off. I said that all units, including artillery units, had some of the weaponry and hardware on standby which can react almost immediately. In professional terms, this is called permanent measures of combat-readiness and those measures are in place in every unit. When you observe a mobile mortar and when you observe fire being launched from a mobile mortar, as soon as the report is sent that a mobile mortar opened fire, a duty officer who doesn't necessarily have to be the commander -- so the duty officer can order the use of an appropriate piece of weaponry that can adequately react to that mobile mortar fire. I have to tell you when it come to Zlatiste, my zone of responsibility, and when it comes to Osmice, the view of Sarajevo from those two areas is fantastic and we did not even need any optical sights to observe any such movements or activities. And why did I mention the military hospital? Because it was in Marin Dvor, immediately behind the front line, behind the military hospital through the tunnel, through Gorice, is where traffic used to run before the war. And during the war that was exclusively used as shelter for such hardware for the tank that was there all the time and opened fire on our positions, for example, in Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, that's interesting --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just -- lines 8 [Interpretation] On line 8 "Grbavica" is missing as an urban part and the witness mentioned both Trebevic and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, that additional information is interesting, but to go back to the question I asked you it was about whether this process you've described for approval of engagement of a target had to be followed in the case of every response to a mobile mortar, and I take from your answer that the answer is sometimes but not always; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. However, you failed to notice that I'm talking about the chain of command and I said that there were officers on duty as well as hardware on duty. It doesn't have to be the commander who approves that. It can be the duty officer who is always there, always on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how -- what kind of measures would you take, since these mobile mortars you've described would be located near civilian buildings, what kind of measures would you take in your response to protect against collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that wherever the mortar is, wherever it is it's a legitimate target according to the international rule of war. Whoever opens fire from a building, irrespective of who the inhabitants are, whether they are civilians or not, this is a legitimate military target. They mustn't do that; still, they did it, in order to provoke a response and then the deaths of civilians would be represented as torturising the civilians of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, could you repeat your last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. The weaponry would be placed near facilities such as hospitals and buildings inhabited by civilians. Fire would be opened from there in order to provoke a response by the VRS. When such a response was provoked, there were indeed collateral casualties and damage. And then in reports the deaths of civilians would be represented as purposeful sniping, terrorising, and shelling of the citizens of Sarajevo. And I repeat, according to the rules of war every target from which fire is opened is a legitimate military target, irrespective of what it contains; what's in that building, for example. If fire is opened from that building, it becomes a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, could you kindly and carefully listen to the question and try to answer that question. The question was not whether mobile mortars were legitimate targets or not. In your statement, para 32, you stated that when executing combat actions and opening fire at military targets located in civilian zones, you said: "We took measures to reduce collateral civilian damages." So Ms. Edgerton's question was whether -- what kind of measures did you take when responding to such mobile mortars? It sounds as if you didn't take any measures. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it a while ago. Measures were as follows: Nobody could open fire without an order issued either by the duty officer or the unit commander, and that's a full measure because the unit commander did not fire blindly. First elements had to be calculated. Everything had to be put in order for a specific target to be hit and not the entire area, and that's the most important measure that protects from collateral damage. Second of all, it was up to the commander to decide whether to respond because fire was not always returned, it was returned only when the lives of the people were at risk, either on the positions or the civilians in the area of Grbavica. It could happen or it could be construed that after a mortar fire was opened there was a prolonged fire on the area. If the effect was not immediate, there were no measures taken, these were the only measures that could be taken. There were no other measures that could be put in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've kind of referred to targets and you just said everything had to be put in order for a specific target to be hit and not the entire area. So maybe you could explain, did you actually -- did you have target lists or was the identification of targets kind of an ad hoc thing?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every unit in front of it had the list of targets as those targets from which they could expect threats, and then it was recorded on maps very precisely. All the elements were identified in order to allow those units to open fire on those targets in a fast and effective manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you just said "all the elements were identified," so maybe you could tell us what the target lists looked like. What information did you have about the targets?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it simply: Our targets were units in front of us. The basic principle was for the artillery to target artillery, and infantry would target infantry, and anti-tank units engaged the enemy's anti-tank units. That was the rule for the engagement and for the selection of targets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In lines 6 through 9 the witness said the elements were measured before fire was opened, before an operation was launched, which probably means or wanted to say much in advance. Maybe Madam Edgerton could verify with the witness whether he indeed said that the elements were identified without action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacevic, do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what is known as the preparation of the battle-field. Everything is calculated in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That might have been interpreted as "in a fast and effective manner." Yes. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just talking about targets and the information you had about the targets, you talk in your statement about the presence of civilians in ABiH-held territory. Does that factor onto your target lists at all?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How? Do you put that information on your target list?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply. If this was simply a manoeuvre ground, not an urban area, one infantry platoon would be a legitimate target for an artillery battery, for example. Since that platoon was in a settled area, it was not a legitimate target for artillery fire because if it had been it would have resulted in a massacre of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't quite see that you answered my question at all. Do you put information about civilians and the presence of civilians on your target lists? How do people know whether there are civilians located in the area of a military target?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see to a large extent from the position. You could see which buildings were inhabited by civilians. You could observe that. You could see that. Second of all, on our side we had a lot of displaced Serbs who were engaged as a labour force in the BiH units. They were used to dig trenches, and then after that they would sometimes defect, they would escape to our side. And when they reached us, they would provide us with the exact information as to what was where because they had been employed as labour force in those exact areas. Based on such information, we corrected our own elements, the elements that we had previously identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you had nothing more up-to-date than that? Because the information from people who cross over to your side gets pretty stale pretty quickly. In fact, it's stale as soon as they across over to your side.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, the number of those who crossed over to our side was continuous. They kept on coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you put the information from those people about civilians in your target lists?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that we faired with caution when it came to that information. We did not take all of that information at its face value. We did not dare blindly trust such statements and information because some of that could have been a trap.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often did you update your target lists?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a continuous process.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that must have been very difficult without forward observation because you'd given evidence earlier that you actually had no forward observation.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have forward observation. However, I repeat, from Trebevic, for those who know the area and the city, without any optical sights one could determine what the situation in Sarajevo was pretty accurately. And not only from Trebevic, but from all the elevations around Sarajevo and within Sarajevo itself. Sarajevo is a relatively small city, but truth be told it was rather densely inhabited. And in certain areas of Sarajevo the front line could be reached with a simple infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if Sarajevo was densely inhabited, as you've just said, maybe I could ask this: Did you have any no-fire zones? Was there any area -- any area of the city not to be targeted?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what were they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Cengic Vila, it never came under fire. It was well sheltered from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that was a no-fire zone for you. Were there any others or was that the only one?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the only one, but only from Cengic Vila fire was never opened against us. There was no front line in Cengic Vila.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, so this wasn't actually a no-fire zone; it was a zone in which you hadn't identified any military objects?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cengic Vila was mostly inhabited by civilians, there were no institutions, there was no military, and there was no need to open fire on Cengic Vila. Nobody really felt the need to open fire on Cengic Vila or any such areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd like to go on to another area in your statement. You indicated at paragraph 34 that: "There had been instances of individuals opening fire without us knowing whether that fire had caused any consequences. In any case, we punished such breaches of discipline." Now, that was from paragraph 34 of your statement. What kind of breaches of discipline and cases of individuals opening fire without you knowing whether that had caused any consequences are you actually talking about?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you some very specific examples. When a soldier, for example, gets drunk and then, irrespective of his position, he opens fire from a weapon that he had been issued with, he can provoke a reaction from the other side. And that reaction may have consequences. This would be the most common example of a breach of discipline. There are also cases when a soldier on the front line of his own will for reasons known to nobody else but him opens random fire and causes damage on the enemy side and provokes reaction against either our unit or the city itself. The following example of the lack of -- of the breach of discipline is the wilful abandonment of one's unit or the front line. Of course there is also theft or similar breaches of discipline. I don't want to go any further, but according to all our rules that were obeyed in peacetime and in war time, such people would be processed according to the disciplinary rules and the rules of engagement during the war. It depended on the gravity of the crime what the punishment would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did any one of those incidents, those breaches, deal with the killing by gun-fire or injury by gun-fire or sniper fire or -- of the civilians by your forces, civilians in Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely - and that's what I said in my statement - what exactly happened over there because I was unable to go there. However, there is one thing that I know because I saw it most often on television because I was able to watch BH TV channel, I can believe that but I don't have, necessarily, to believe it because I know that many things were staged. There were such instances, however, I don't know to what extent those were truthful ones and it's not up to me to judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about shelling? Did you ever investigate a case of shelling civilians in Bosnian-held territory, shelling by your forces?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not investigate any shelling because I didn't have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer a little bit more slowly, please, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not conduct such investigations because I didn't have any artillery pieces in my unit, and I am an infantry officer and I wouldn't be competent to carry out any expert investigation relating to artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you say "unit," right now you're talking about your battalion. Does the same apply from your time when you served in brigade command?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was serving on the brigade command, I also couldn't be involved in the artillery matters because that was the duty of the chief of artillery. He was a professional who proposes a decision for engagement to the commander with respect to artillery. So he was chief of artillery and part of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in neither your battalion nor in your brigade were you aware of any investigations whatsoever conducted in cases of shelling and sniping civilians by VRS forces in Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the brigade I know, definitely know, that the chief of artillery was maintaining constant contact with UNPROFOR observation team --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish, please -- which was deployed at the command post of the artillery unit, and everything they did was something that the commander of artillery unit was aware of, the chief of artillery was aware of, and the brigade commander was aware of. As an infantry officer, I myself wasn't involved in these processes because I don't have the necessary skills relating to the use of artillery. As for the battalion, I didn't have any artillery pieces and therefore I couldn't have done any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it from your answer that that's a no and we'll move on. We've talked about or you've talked about in your statement that Bosnian attack on the 6th of January, 1994 - and that's at paragraph 24 of your statement - and just to refresh your memory, I'll read you that sentence. You talk -- you say: "On our side we had such cases, notably on 6 January 1994, when Muslims executed an attack on the Jewish cemetery and the Vrbanja bridge." So I'd like to read you something about this attack on 6 January 1994 and that's from 65 ter 23902.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have to intervene. Madam Edgerton, with all due respect, gave an answer instead of the witness. The witness didn't say that there were no investigations at the level of the brigade, but, rather, that that was done by professional people in co-operation with UNPROFOR. Your conclusion when you said the answer is no refers not -- only to the battalion and not to the brigade. I'm talking about line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered that: "... everything they did was something that the command of artillery unit was aware of, the chief of artillery was aware of, and the brigade commander was aware of." He didn't refer to any specific example, so that's why Ms. Edgerton said "no" and the witness didn't respond to that comment, but it's a comment. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 23902, please. We should have an English original as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a UN military observer because you've just been talking about a UN military observers, this is a UN military observer sitrep for Sector Sarajevo for 5 and 6 January 1994. And over on paragraph 7 of that document, page 2, in English, and I'm not sure quite which paragraph in B/C/S, the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S and it will go over on to page 3. Could we go to page 2 in English. Thank you. I'll read you what paragraph 7(a) of this document says on the situation in Sarajevo for the day of this attack you referred to. It says: "The UNPROFOR units reported that the BiH launched an offensive into the Serb-held areas of Grbavica today. It is as yet unclear as to what if any ground has been gained by the BiH. This action led" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Next page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just wait until the next page comes up before I continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "... this action led to the Serb forces issuing an ultimatum on the local radio station, stating that unless Bosnian forces ceased the attack then a massive retaliation would take place in the form of an artillery attack. The whole town of Sarajevo was put on alert of the impending attack ..." So your forces' response to this attack on 6 January that you talk about in your statement was to threaten the massive retaliation against the city as a whole; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my response. I don't know -- this came from. I was not in charge of the radio, so therefore I couldn't dictate what the radio would broadcast.
