I cannot comment on everything that was happening all around Sarajevo. I can only speak about Grbavica and what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if that's the case, when you say at paragraph 27 of your evidence "we did not fire at civilians ...," you're only referring to the situation with your battalion in Grbavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a while ago, when you asked me about the brigade I'm answering about the brigade and also when you asked me about the battalion I'm talking about the battalion. Nothing beyond that. Sarajevo is a rather wide area and I'm reluctant to comment on what other people did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can remove that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 27 of your statement, you said: "The members of my unit were perfectly aware of what consequences might befall the Serb army if indiscriminate fire was opened at civilian targets." I'm thinking of showing you some documents in that regard but before I do that, what do you understand "indiscriminate fire" means?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indiscriminate fire on Sarajevo meant uncontrolled firing of artillery projectiles randomly without any specific target in mind or without any need for that. Indiscriminate fire would also involve any senseless firing upon people just for the purpose of terrorising them. At some periods, anything that would disrupt everyday life and work would also be senseless unless it posed a threat to a unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to P15 -- pardon me, P01587, a UN military observer daily sitrep for Sector Sarajevo for 7 and 8 January 1994. I'm going to read you what this document says at page 2, paragraph 2 -- sorry. Could you go back to the first page. It appeared -- thank you. If you could go down to paragraph 2 it refers to 175 outgoing mixed rounds from Serb-held territory causing 35 wounded, including seven women and one child, and ten killed, including two women and one child, and says that: "Approximately 50 per cent of impacts recorded were on the front line. The remainder were directed at residential areas or areas of regular civilian usage." Now could you please go over to paragraph 9 which I think is on the second page. Paragraph 9 says: "It appears that the reason for the high level of casualties inside Sarajevo is due to the shelling by the BSA," Bosnian Serb army, "of guns of an area used extensively by civilians as a means of avoiding sniper areas. This area is always very busy with civilian foot track [sic]." So what you've just heard from me now as reported in this document, does that fit within your definition of indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I can't see from this document where this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that make any difference to your being able to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this I can conclude that this happened on the front line of the 1st Corps of the ABH and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS. This is a very large area. This does not show where these casualties happened and how, and since I wasn't there I can hardly comment on it. I can only offer you my opinion. This is a report that doesn't say much to me as an officer. Why is that? Because we said a while ago that the separation lines in urban areas, that close to them or on the very lines themselves, civilians live. It doesn't say that civilian targets were engaged here but only that there were some civilians killed as well. And I just said a minute ago that any action can result in civilian casualties in urban areas, any action whatsoever. Secondly, I noticed that the term "sniper fire" is being used out of the context and meaning of any proper military definition of "sniper fire." It seems that every short fire is ascribed to snipers, and that is not the case. The snipers constitute the fewest number of members of a unit. However, every action is described as being sniper fire. I have no doubts that this is the correct number of casualties, but we need more specific descriptions and more details saying whether the civilians were really the target or whether this was a result of a mistake. So it's difficult to conclude what exactly happened here. So this speaks about casualties on one side only. I think that there was fire coming from both sides, so if there are no casualties from the other side, in my mind this is a one-sided report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What would you do if there was a mistake and civilians in Bosnian-held territory were killed or injured when - as you've said earlier - you had no logs or reports back on what happened with the target -- when the target was engaged?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that if we are talking about something that I didn't do, I would say from where I'm sitting now that I would act according to the rules, which means obeying disciplinary rules and criminal code, nothing else. That was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to another area. It's related to paragraph 16 of your statement where you said: "Later in the war all 80-millimetre and higher-calibre weapons were removed to a distance 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo and were controlled by UNPROFOR." Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we could have a look at the map that's P1593, please. And it's a map from -- obtained from the VRS archives in Banja Luka in 2006 reflecting the 20-kilometre exclusion zone around Sarajevo. And could my colleague please go to the very centre of the city where there's a T marked and enlarge the two red boxes below that T that appear on the right and immediately below it. Brigadier, this map depicts with legends and keys the weapons held at weapons collection points inside the 20-kilometre zone and outside the 20-kilometre zone. And could you just enlarge further those two red boxes so that the brigadier can read it, and probably one more. Now, you see that in the area of Lukavica Tilava there's a weapons collection point or area where ten 120-millimetre mortars are housed or maintained, two 105-millimetre howitzers, two VBR Plamen 128-millimetre multiple rocket-launchers, 15 T55 tanks. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could my colleague just go up to the red square just above this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A weapons collection point in Grbavica this red square shows that four 82-millimetre mortars; five 60 -- sorry, I correct my own mistake, 82-millimetre BaT is the acronym; five 60-millimetre mortars; four 82-millimetre mortars; one Top 76-millimetre B1 gun; and one T55 tank, among other things, are maintained at a weapons collection point in Grbavica, both locations far inside the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. So now having seen this map, do you still stand by what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is correct. The pieces of artillery that were pulled out to the area 20 kilometre of Sarajevo remained in the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska. These assets referred to here were those that were collected really and at specific locations, and they were no longer in our hands. We could only gain access to them with the permission of UNPROFOR. Because this implies the weapons that were collected under the auspices of UNPROFOR and there is a major distinction between those weapons and the other weapons that one has in one's hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But actually, Brigadier, the establishment of the total exclusion zone didn't decrease the combat-readiness of your artillery at all, did it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, considerably.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at 65 ter 23926, please. Brigadier, this is a document dated May 1995 which lists the artillery assets ready to provide fire support for planned SRK actions that month, and it shows clearly where your brigade assets were located. In item 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it very strange I can't find the English translation for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do as well. Just a moment, please, Your Honours -- your indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the date, please, and all the other necessary elements of the document, such as who the author is and who the signatory is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The date's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may come. If we see the next page there is a signature, but I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the translation just now been released. My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, some dates on second page, 2. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back over to the first page and I'll wait for my colleagues to get the English translation called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's uploaded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it shows in your brigade's area of responsibility the location of artillery and other assets. The fire support for the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade is four 120-millimetre -- or it includes four 120-millimetre mortars from the region of Palez; 76-millimetre B1 gun from the area of the barracks at Zlatiste; and two T55 tanks from the areas of Zlatiste and Vrace. So this shows, Brigadier, pretty clearly that your brigade's combat-readiness wasn't affected at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is a prediction. This is not what is actually happening. In order for these assets to arrive in the area specified here, they first have to be taken out and that cannot happen without that being recorded. If force were used to get hold of those weapons, I'm not sure whether this would pass in Sarajevo unnoticed. This is something that is anticipated. This hasn't been done in actual fact and it's -- just indicates the necessity for these assets to be located there. Those assets had not been at these positions prior to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page in Serbian to see what's written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From which date, 14 May 1995, I see that this is a preparation for defence from the announced offensive when the Muslim forces were going to try to break out of Sarajevo. That's when the offensive started and lasted until the end of the war. This is the objective for the defence and the task to cut off the road towards Trebevic. I see the date is 14 May 1995. In the middle of this month, the offensive of Muslim forces from Sarajevo started on all fronts and lasted until the end of August when a cease-fire occurred, and that was the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go on now to 65 ter 23921, please, a document from the VRS Main Staff signed by General Mladic on the regrouping of fire support in and outside the 20-kilometre zone. Now, at the paragraph entitled "positive solutions," which is on page 2 of the English and in B/C/S at the bottom of the first page, we see that within the perimeter of the 20-kilometre zone the fire support equipment was grouped with the possibility of artillery support for companies in the first line of defence and sectors for the regrouping of equipment outside the 20-kilometre zone were chosen with the possibility of use and speedy transfer of the focus of fire support to another axis. The armoured mechanised units of your brigade, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, are trained and drilled for operating the available equipment and can start it up or use it on the given or chosen axes within one and a half hours. So it seems clear here that General Mladic himself finds the establishment of the total exclusion zone does not decrease the combat-readiness of your artillery at all.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can suppose that at the highest level talks were held that weapons be returned to units because of the obvious danger from the announced offensive of the Muslim forces for the final show-down with the forces of the VRS in the area of Sarajevo. To be quite honest, I don't know the outcome of those talks, but according to this order which I see for the first time I see that those weapons were still where they were - under supervision - and the plan envisages their use which is quite logical and legitimate. At a certain point when there is a danger, the time is reduced, these weapons should be recovered as soon as possible. Certain positions should be occupied. That's how I understand this document. I see it for the first time, but this is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have that as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more document -- Just your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go on to another area. You gave evidence, paragraph 15 of your statement, that you had no knowledge to the effect that the final objective for Sarajevo of the Serbian authorities was a division of the city. And I'd like to show you another document by General Mladic, P3052 dated 14 December 1993. It's called supplement to directive 6. Now, this document issued on the basis of a decision dated 14 December 1993, by the highest officials of the Serbian people orders the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps along with other forces to undertake a number of actions. And at the very last line of this first paragraph, we see the objective behind the operation is to provide conditions for the division of Sarajevo into two parts. Seeing this, General, do you stand by your statement in paragraph -- or paragraph 15 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This is a military exit to the dominant features of Hum which was held by the VRS until 17 May 1992, and Hum as we all know is in the central part of Sarajevo. And from there you can have a significant influence on the front line in Sarajevo, a military objective, perfectly realistic, to take control of that area which is - because that is a dominant feature - a hill on which there stands a TV repeater, and with this success the units of the VRS that were in contact with Muslim forces would have a significant burden taken off their shoulders. Putnik and Hrasnica are in the south-west of Sarajevo separated by the airport. They have practically no influence on Sarajevo, but communication between Ilidza would be ensured and the eastern part of Sarajevo which was non-existent at the time because it had turned over the airport in June 1992 and it had no physical contact with the eastern part of Sarajevo anymore. I don't understand this order as a political division of Sarajevo between Serbs and Bosniaks. I understand it as in the first part of the operation taking control of important features and in the second part the integration of two territories in a narrow space - because this is a narrow space - the integration of Putnik and Hrasnica with the eastern part of Sarajevo. That's how I understand this order. I don't understand it as having the objective to separate the Serb and Bosniak parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's an interesting interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add, it was not recorded that the witness said speaking of Hum and that area that it was uninhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that, Mr. Kovacevic? Hum area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is speaking much too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hum, Zuc, and Orlic alike were uninhabited then and still are uninhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is my observation, Mr. Kovacevic, you are speaking a bit too fast for the interpreters to follow. Could you speak a bit slower. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll go on to one final area and it's an area you mentioned at the early part of your statement, paragraph 8, where you said: "At all the positions where I had been not a single offensive action had been executed but exclusively defensive ones. These positions were established at the beginning of the war and they remained as such until the end of the war." And so I'd like you in that regard to have a look at another document, 65 ter 09139. It's a letter from Dragomir Milosevic to Ratko Mladic on 19 May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We need to go over to B/C/S page 4, I think the fifth full paragraph on page 4, and English page 2, the last full paragraph on the page. My page numbering is off, Your Honours. If you could just give me a moment's indulgence, I may move on in the interest of speed. The English page I see in front of me is page 4 and in the English I needed page 2, and in the B/C/S that's page 3 and I need page 2 in the B/C/S. Wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So at the fifth full paragraph on the page on the left-hand side of the screen and in the last full paragraph, the English page on the right-hand side of the screen, Dragomir Milosevic writes to General Mladic: When engaging in combat, I spared myself from nothing. I fought with ... commitment and was involved, personally involved, in, among other things, liberating Soping at Grbavica II and he personally stormed and, together with the police and a platoon of soldiers, liberated the Zlatiste facility, liberated the Bistrik tower and the Mala tower at Mrkovici. He did everything to foil incursions from Sarajevo along any axis. And it was thanks to him that Ozrenska Street was preserved. Now, this language of liberating, does that sound like an offensive or a defensive action to you, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read this - and I believe you have - at this time when this was going on that was 1992. At that time, I was in Pazarici and after that in Blazuj. So I wasn't at these positions. And, if you look at what is offensive and what is defensive, all these features are taken by one squad, Bankovici Kula [phoen] can hold ten people, not more. Zlatiste Kula can hold 15 people. The facility of Osmice is a small restaurant. All these things are along roads. I can understand and I know that the objective was to keep primarily the road from Lukavica towards Pale across Trebevic and that's why these small features were taken. If that's an offensive, then so be it, but I don't see it that way. An offensive is a broader term. The same about Mrkovici, that's on the road from Pretis, Radana -- Radane towards Pale. I've never seen any of these features enumerated here larger than could be taken by a platoon. You cannot call them offensives. It doesn't qualify as an offensive. And, finally, let me say, this line remained identical at the end of the war, almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if that's -- if you think we can't call that an offensive, maybe we'll have another look at another document from Dragomir Milosevic. It's D568, and it's a speech that he gave on the ceremony of presenting the war flags in 1996. And the page that we need to see is page 3 in both languages. Now here General Milosevic says: "We carried out -- furthermore, we carried out operations in order to improve our tactical positions and extend free Serb territories in the areas of Otes, Mojmilo, Zlatiste, Kijev, and then towards Praca and Gosinje." Now, does that characterise offensive or defensive action, extending free Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to sound as a teacher. The term "operation" is used here. Operations are carried out by the largest units and there is no reference here to "combat, battle," as the main terms. None of these features listed here does have a size that cannot be occupied by one company, one infantry company. These are small features, the occupying of which gives a small tactical advantage, but the person who wrote this does not understand terms like "battle, combat" especially "operation." Armies conduct operations. Which forces carried this out? Spreca and Gosinje? I really don't know. I wasn't there so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. How about we look at one last document. It's 65 ter 23939, and it's an order to attack dated 30 November 1992 to the 1st Rajlovac Brigade, which you should be familiar with, Brigadier, because for a period of time in 1992 you commanded the 1st Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that it hasn't been released yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take this on my shoulders completely, Your Honours. It's 23839, and my apologies to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This document in paragraph 1, when it talks about information of the enemy -- about the enemy says: "There are no civilians in the neighbourhood next to the Sokolje mosque but there are in the area from the mosque towards Brijesce." And over this paragraph 3 of the English and still at the bottom of page 1 on the B/C/S, we see the tasks -- can we go back to page 1 of the B/C/S. We see the tasks of the brigade. And there it says: "Our brigade has been instructed to launch an attack from its starting positions to the right of Lemezovo Brdo - Zabrdje - Smiljevici towards Svabino Brdo and Brijesko Brdo, cut off the village, surround the enemy forces in the village of Sokolje, thoroughly mop up the villages of Sokolje, Brijesce, and Brijesko Brdo, reach the Zuc-Skravnik refuse dump-Brijesko Brdo line and link up with our forces in the village of Vecici where it will switch till defence, regroup its forces, built fortifications," et cetera. Now, is this an offensive or a defensive action?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an offensive action of limited nature. I should like you to show a map for us to see what this area looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think you've actually answered my question perfectly clearly. Thank you very much, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can I understand that as saying that I answered in the affirmative, that it's an offensive? I said in fact it was an offensive action of limited nature. It refers to taking control of one feature and that's why I wanted the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber understood your answer. We can move on. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic may take up that issue further in his re-examination. I take it you are not tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I should only like to give the opportunity to General Kovacevic to finish what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are these features: Zuc, Brijesko Brdo, Smetliste [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a sharp point, a wedge, that was going into a populated area of Rajlovac. That's where from the factory Orlovo and the transformer station were exposed to constant fire and we wanted to stop this terrorising. And this sharp point called Sokolje which is about 300 metres wide on the average, we wanted to cut it off and to straighten this line. This is very precise and we can see on the map clearly what is achieved by that. This is a very limited objective. When the entire operation is done, it involves only one platoon. So it can't even be called an operation. It's called improving one's tactical position. That's why I insisted earlier on distinctions between terms such as "combat, action, battle, and operation" and "tactical correction of the line."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your answer. Thank you for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm asking this purely out of my personal curiosity. In paragraph 43 of your statement you stated that among the volunteers in your unit were included the persons from Korea. Do you remember them? Were they from North Korea or South Korea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Kobe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From Kobe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Japan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then "Korea" was written by mistake. I'm sure I said they were from Kobe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Kobe/Korea is probably the reason why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You overlapped with the translation. Your comment was not noted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In our pronunciation, Kobe -- from Kobe or from Korea is only one letter, one sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Kovacevic. On behalf of the Chamber -- before letting the witness go, do you have any comments, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Going back to the associated exhibit that you called our attention to, it may require an explanation from the witness so I just wanted to let the Chamber know this is 1D2337 which is now Exhibit 2332. In fact, the numbers were mixed up and so the number that was referred to in paragraph 49 of his statement reflects a different number, but it's the same document. If you want us to have him confirm that, we can do that, but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So both documents refer to the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're both the same document, yes. I'm informed now that we've uploaded 1D845 -- we've uploaded that same document as 1D8452, but if you would like to have the witness confirm it, we can do that. If it's not necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take your word, Mr. Robinson. So I'd like to thank you on behalf of this Chamber, Mr. Kovacevic, for your coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Now you're free to go, but we will rise all together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.00 -- oh, I'm sorry, quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please take your seat and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Skrba. Shall I address you "colonel" or "general"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: "Skrba" will be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court 1D6030.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the statement that you gave to the Defence team and is this a statement that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Not in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Has anyone read this statement to you in English and does it accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting Mr. Karadzic. I think this witness, Your Honour, Mr. President, will need a 90(E) warning and perhaps it should be given now before he starts giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Skrba, before you go further I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Under this rule, which is Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Chamber if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. I mean by "incriminate" that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first I hear of this, and I will abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Instead of this statement, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give me the same answers as contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, can I ask for 1D6030 be admitted into evidence along with other documents, that is to say the totality of 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Witness's Rule 92 ter statement will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it you are tendering two documents as associated exhibits? Any objection, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, they will be also admitted. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour 65 ter 1D8567 will be Exhibit D2342 and 65 ter 1D8568 will be Exhibit D2343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like now to read the summary of Mr. Skrba's statement in English. [In English] Dusan Skrba was born on 24 of February 1949 in Kasindol, Ilidza municipality, Sarajevo. Before the war he worked in the Sarajevo work unit of Univerzalpromet Prokuplje. He served the army in 1970/1971 in Zadar in the school for reserve officers, combat arms artillery. Dusan Skrba saw a line-up of the Green Berets before the war started in October or November 1991 outside of Sarajka department store in the centre of Sarajevo. He also had knowledge that the Patriotic League had had a line-up in Hrasnica in October 1991. On March the 15th, 1992, he was called by the JNA to report to Slavisa Vajner-Cica barracks in Lukavica where he was charged with manning establishment units. Starting on April the 4th, 1992, infantry attacks by Muslim units on the barracks took place on a daily basis. All types of infantry weapons including rifle, grenades, and hand-held rocket-launchers and hand-grenades were used. During the crisis in May 1992 connected to the pull-out of JNA members from barracks in the city of Sarajevo and cadets from the Marsal Tito barracks, Dusan Skrba was ordered to prepare in the event of an attack on the units and the pull-out routes. When Muslim forces attacked the Marsal Tito barracks he was ordered to open fire on those units at Marin Dvor. On 27th of May, 1992, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade was formed. This brigade consisted mostly of hardware and was insufficiently manned. Dusan Skrba became the commander of the mixed artillery battalion. The zone of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade was from Kozja Cuprija bridge and Bembasa to the old airport and the Zeljeznica river as it is marked on the associated exhibit 1D08567. On 1st of July, 1992, UN observers were deployed to his command post and remained there until the end of the war. Every time before opening fire Dusan Skrba would inform the UN observers and show the points from which Muslim forces had attacked. He would submit a report on the spot to the UN members in each instance fire was opened. The UN observers never complained to him about his reports, his work or the work of his units. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' objectives were to protect its front lines which were in Serbian ethnic areas and to prevent the breakthrough of the 1st Corps for Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina outside of the city section of Sarajevo under Muslim control. This would have made available a large number of enemy personnel in other fronts. During the war, according to his knowledge, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps conducted exclusively defensive actions, with the sole exception of Operation Lukavica 93, the goal of which was to join the Herzegovina and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps towards the mountains. Dusan Skrba had information and data that units of the 1st Corps of BH army were deployed in the depth of the territory of the city and that they also encompassed civilian zones of the section of the city under the control of the Muslim authorities, such as Velesici, Ciglane, Bjelave, City Hall, Dobrinja IIIB and Bistrik. His unit and he personally always took every measure not to open fire on civilian targets in the city. Fire was to be opened exclusively at observed firing positions and military targets for the purpose of self-defence all on the order of the superior command in respect of specific military targets. Neither he nor any other members of his unit or their subordinate or superior commands ever intended to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians in the territory under Muslim control or attack means of public transportation. They never received or issued any verbal or written orders to that effect. Although the brigade has a number of aerial bombs in stock, they were never used in the zone of responsibility of this unit. Regarding incidents in which three mortar shells landed in the area of Alipasino Polje on January the 22nd, 1994, Dusan Skrba identifies as the Butmir agricultural state what the Defence considers to be the most probable place of firing. He also states that fire could be opened from that direction at Nedzarici and Alipasino Polje. Regarding incident in which a salvo of three 120-millimetre mortar shells hit the Dobrinja residential area on the 4th of February, 1994, Dusan Skrba claims that no fire was opened that day and could not have been opened without his command which he did not issue and without it being reported to the UNPROFOR observers. Regarding incidents on Safeta Zajke Street and Majdanska Street on 24th of May, 1995, Dusan Skrba claims that no aerial bomb was ever fired from Prljevo or Lukavica. Regarding Markale II incident, Dusan Skrba claims that fire could not have been opened that day from 120-mortars since all of 120-mortars and the higher-calibre weapons were not in the hands of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps but are either out of the 20-kilometres zone or in the UNPROFOR control. I don't have questions, additional questions for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. During the cross-examination I'm going to be using a number of maps, and for -- of course they're all uploaded in e-court. But for the ease of the participants, I have hard copies and I would ask the usher's assistance to deliver these, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For planning purposes, can I know how long you would take, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would believe that at least two full sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We apologise for taking our copies of the maps before Your Honours. It's like eating before the guests, but anyway apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have D2342, please, in e-court. Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My name is Kim West. I'm one of the attorneys with the Office of the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you a series of questions today and very likely it will go to Monday as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. In front of you on the screen is a map I know you've seen before. And if we could zoom into the area right in the middle. This is a map that was provided to us noting your area of responsibility. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Marked in colour red?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we could zoom into that area in colour red.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is this an area that you marked noting your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, that would be it. That's our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And this is quite small, so may I have 65 ter 09390E, and what I've done is I've just taken a more detailed map so we can go through it a bit easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I know Mr. Reid is busy multi-tasking there but we would like to receive the list of exhibits that they're going to use during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, yesterday I introduced the larger map. This is based off of that same map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, now looking at this, this is just a blow-up or what we just saw, and you on the screen in front of you have the ability to circle spots that I direct you to. And if we could ensure that the witness can do that. First place I want you to circle is your command post. Sir, you see the location right in the middle? It's Uzdojnice. I've mutilated that word, but it's right in the middle. Can you tell us what's there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Uzdojnice was a command post of the mixed artillery battalion and also of the units that were deployed in that area. Shall I mark it as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: So that's the command post. Do I need to mark where other units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So tell me -- can you mark the area of Lukavica and tell us what was in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, Lukavica was in front of our forward line, and this area here is in front of the Slavisa Vajner-Cica and Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks. This is Energoinvest. And further on you have the Cica barracks, but you can't see it on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So put a circle around Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I can only circle the industrial part of Energoinvest and also the electrical engineering faculty, and what you see here is part of the industrial complex of Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, on this map as well towards the right-hand lower corner we see a place called Tilava. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was located there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: An infirmary was in Tilava and the local commune centre. Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can sign your name on this and put the date as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Today is the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5933 , Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I make a suggestion while we still have it here. The witness said that only the faculty and Energoinvest company can be seen here. Can we then mark these areas with letters F and E in order to make sure that these were not barracks but rather other types of facilities. So can we put a rectangle instead of a circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Could you put E and F.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, was any particular headquarters located at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: What do you mean at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, in regard to -- well, let me back up. In regard to the place where you were located the most, is that one of the circles you put on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, yes, Uzdojnice and Palovac, the subordinate command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how often --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: And there was also the corps command post, but it cannot be seen in this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Skrba, we know that you were involved in artillery matters for the 1st Sarajevo Militarised Brigade command, but can you tell us from whom you took your orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: We were receiving orders from the artillery chief from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you also receive orders from the artillery corps command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: No, not directly. Everything went through the artillery chief of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And starting in 1992, can you tell us the name of that person, the person from whom you took those orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Captain, or rather, on the 27th of May, when I became the commander of the MAD Savo Simic was my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at some point did your superior commander change?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: The brigade commander remained the same person and Savo Simic took a new position towards the end of 1994 so I took over both duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, the orders that you received, they were both in writing and verbal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Only in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only in writing. Thank you for that clarification. In paragraph 14 of your report you speak about the order of the superior command in respect of specific military targets. In that regard can you tell us -- describe for us how specific, how detailed, military targets would be in these orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Every target had to be marked and described in terms of its size, location, and what kind of enemy assets were there, whether there was manpower or equipment and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when you received orders to target something, this is the type of specific information you would expect to receive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: We always expected specific information, the location, the place, and the size of the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why was that detail important to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Those details were important so that we should be able to plan what kind of artillery fire we should open, individual fire with one weapon or group fire with a whole unit using weapons of a specific calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P1511, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to look at an example of not an actual order but an example of some language, and this is not a -- you will not have seen this before, but I want to know if this is consistent with your experience. This is an intercept dated the 29th of May, 1992, and the Trial Chamber has heard some evidence on this. It's a discussion -- it's a conversation between General Mladic and a person named Potpara. That name, Potpara - excuse my pronunciation - do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. In the course of this conversation Mladic is asking the other individual: "Mladic: Is he shooting at you?" Potpara says: "No, not at the moment. "Mladic: Are you shooting? "Potpara: We returned fire. "Mladic: Returned fire! Excellent! Where?" And then Potpara says: "Up there, towards the museum and towards the hospital up there and Crni Vrh. "Mladic: Yes. What weapons did you use? "Potpara: 82. "Mladic: 82. Did you shoot at the target? "Potpara: Those who were observing ... "Mladic: Pardon? "Potpara: These observers told us it was good. "Mladic: Fire at ... at a good target. "Potpara: Okay. "Mladic: Don't let them well ... disturb you. "Potpara: Good. "Mladic: As soon as the mother fuckers attack you, fire at them. Can you hit the railway station? "Potpara: Yes, we can. "Mladic: Hit them with something. And scatter them around. "Potpara: Okay. "Mladic: Bye." Sir, my question for you regards this language "scatter them around." Would you consider that language to be detailed enough in describing a target?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this does not relate to me because I did not have command over this 82. That weapon was not at the disposal of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed. And as I said earlier, this si not a conversation that I expected you to recognise. I am using it only as an example to talk about what you mentioned as detailed targeting language. So, for example, the language "scatter them around," if you had received an order like that, would you consider that to have been detailed enough for you to pick a target?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I never got an order of that kind and I don't think it's precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the process by which you challenged an order?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I asked for a written approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I mean what --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: With the proviso that if I asked for an explanation or approval in writing for taking a target, I always made sure through my observers and artillery observers, our people on our forward lines on higher ground who did reconnaissance and scouting, if they gave me a report and assurance of what kind of target that was, only then could an order be issued to prepare fire and open fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you do that on every occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I could say 99 per cent of cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the process by which you deployed the people underneath you, your men. For example, did you have fixed firing locations and did you deploy them out to those locations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Artillery's an idiosyncratic unit with special training and of course at every position we had to have trained people able to operate that weapon and people who were able to observe targets, prepare co-ordinates, so that we could prepare fire and only then proceed to open fire and aim at a certain target because there are several ways of opening fire: There's simple preparation, abbreviated preparation, and full preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll get there. But just tell me, how many different firing locations did you have in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: In this place I had four units and four firing positions, and I didn't change them throughout the war until we relocated 20 kilometres back.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have again 65 ter 09390E, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to locate your firing positions, but, first, tell me, is this map too small an area for you to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: All right. I'll show this within smaller lines. It can fit in.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I see four lines. Do those represent your four firing positions until they were relocated?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those four, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And for how long did they remain in those four places?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Until we moved 20 kilometres further behind, further from the circle around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell me when you did that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: That was sometime in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So up until August of 1995, those were your four permanent firing locations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during -- from 1992 until August of 1995, were there any other firing positions anywhere else in your area of responsibility over which you had command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: In my area of firing responsibility, there were no other artillery units but those four.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you sign this and again put the date on it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Just a little correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can delete it with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And may this have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be saved and given the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, in paragraph 10 of your report you talk about the 1st ABiH Corps and the type of weapons that they had. But I now would like to talk about the type of weapons that you had. Can you tell us whether you had any mortars?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Twelve pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What else did you have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: MD30 howitzers, 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 122-millimetres, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six pieces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: And Weber 128-millimetres, four pieces, four.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What else did you have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you have any multiple-barrelled rocket-launchers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: That is it VBR, the last thing I mentioned, 128-millimetres, four pieces of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry, it says something different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, if you don't mind could we take a short break of five minutes. --- Break taken at 1.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today's session, the Chamber will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his urgent personal business. By the way, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We received some responses to our motions for protective measures for witnesses that are coming up in the month of November, and we would like to advise the Chamber that it's going to be our practice to contact the witness after we receive the response of the Prosecution to see if there's any further information they wish us to provide to the Chamber; and if so, to seek leave to reply so that you have that information. So I would appreciate it if you would give us a few days. We expect we would file on Monday any replies, but if you would hold off on making your decisions until we have had some opportunity to reply and that would generally be our practice throughout the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's been noted. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, when we stopped we were speaking about rocket-launchers, and you indicated that your unit had four. Can you tell us what was their purpose? In what type of situation did you use a rocket-launcher?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: They are rarely used and for them you need a lot of ammunition so that during the war we didn't use them much, perhaps once or twice, and that's all. They're used solely to neutralise enemy personnel on attack, infantry attack of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless you had four; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you said you've used them once or twice. Please tell us about the two occasions when you used them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Once it was used by the JNA while they were still in Lukavica before they left for Serbia. I believe it was on the 3rd or 4th of May. I didn't command or decide there. And once or twice in 1993 we used them in the direction of Mount Igman when we performed the operation Lukavac 93.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so in your memory you've now spoken about three situations where they were used. Is that the extent of your memory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, there were those three situations, otherwise during the whole war they were used in only three situations regarding my positions and my weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so we say regarding your positions. Are we talking about those four firing positions you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you have one at each of those firing positions or did you have -- or how were they spread out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: All the four were in one place as I marked on that last document. They were grouped in one place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 24 you said: "On August 28th there were no 120-millimetre mortars and those mortars and those of larger calibre which were in my zone of responsibility had already been relocated outside the city of Sarajevo." In August of 1995 I understand your testimony is that 120-millimetre was located outside, but what about the smaller mortars? Were they still within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: They were not in my area of responsibility. They belonged to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless there were smaller mortars within the area south of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Battalion commanders deployed them and positioned them in their area of responsibility. I did not have insight either in their deployment or their number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally what you used 120-millimetre mortars for? What was their best purpose?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: 120-millimetres are mainly used to destroy personnel on slopes, be it forward or back slants because it can land a shell from up high.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us typically when you fired from 120-millimetre mortar, how many times did you fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: It depended on the target and on the type of attack. It also depended on the trajectory of the shell from the place it was fired to the target. It could be one minute, two minute, five-minute distance. You could adjust that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But it would be -- would it be normal to fire only once?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "only once"? You mean only one shell?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Only rarely would it be one shell. It would be one or two or more. Only if you had previously fired at the same target would you fire just one shell in the second go, but normally before that you would have to check all the firing elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you said that they were mainly used to destroy personnel. What type of ordnance did you mainly use to destroy buildings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, you would need tanks or Maljutkas for that or other ordnance and other hardware, cannons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 12 of your statement you said that: "According to my knowledge, the SRK conducted exclusively defensive actions." So in other words, does this mean that you only fired in retaliation to ABiH fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Exclusively in response to the BiH army fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so let's talk about that response time. Can you tell us -- can you walk us through the process of your response. When you're first fired upon, what was the first thing that you did?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: The first thing was -- I received report from the observation post that fire was open on the forward line. My observers would inform me about that. And then directly from the brigade command, I would receive a report that in a certain sector an attack was either expected or was underway. It would have been either an artillery or an infantry attack. And when those two reports corresponded, then we determined the location of the target, the co-ordinates of the target, we calculated the elements, and the time that lapsed would be five, ten, or ten minutes. And then if the shelling continued, then we would respond in order to calm the situation down. It would be one shell first, and then the observers would observe and see whether that first shell fell where we wanted it to fall. If not, then we corrected our firing elements in order to proceed. In 90 per cent of the situations, we used only one piece to fire our shell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intervention on the transcript. The witness said: We fired one shell in order to calm the situation down, not only to correct the firing elements, but also to calm the situation down and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe it was, but we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's back up. You said before you fired your first -- the first response, about five or ten -- it would take about five or ten minutes. So there would be a short period of time before you retaliated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the first thing you'd hear about it would be from your observers; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then you'd hear from the brigade command that there was an attack expected or underway?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Or I would inform them. I would inform the duty officer in the command, because I had my observers so I knew what was going on, I would inform them and I would await instructions as to what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in other words, you would confirm that there had been a firing and then you would determine the location of the target and then you would retaliate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: And I requested their approval. I expected them to tell me what to do, whether to respond with fire or to wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 14 of your statement, you talk a little bit more about this, and there you say you took measures to not open fire on civilians. And then down in paragraph 16 -- and maybe we can have both the B/C/S and English of paragraph 16, please. You continue to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told there's no B/C/S version, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there's a draft statement that has a B/C/S translation of this paragraph, but it's under a different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And perhaps that 65 ter number might be 1D05641 for the B/C/S version. I think it would be helpful if we could have the B/C/S version of this paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you see this in front of you as well. On the left is your version and on the right is the English. This paragraph begins: "We had standing orders to the effect that fire must not be opened on civilian targets in the city. I, personally, and my unit during combat actions and when opening fire on military targets which were in civilian zones took measures to reduce collateral civilian casualties." And then the next sentence is: "For instance, if tank fire from the sector Velesici or Ciglane was opened at us we would respond with proportionate fire at the place from which the fire on our unit was opened." Mr. Skrba, is this proportionate fire that you speak about in that sentence, is that what you meant by measures, when you spoke about the measures you would take?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, yes, if they fired two or three shells we retaliated with one or two shells in our turn, in order to stop them from proceeding with their activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if they -- and if they fired from a tank, you would return with a tank fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, our tank could not reach those places from which they opened tank fire. That's why I tended to use 122-millimetre howitzer instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I say "tank" because that's the example you use in this sentence, but if you -- if they fired with 122-millimetre how -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Well, they opened fire from Velesici and Ciglane from tank and from howitzers and they fired on our forward positions, and then if we did not return fire immediately they would just go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But let's go back to what we were talking about which is proportionate fire. For example, if they fired from a 130-millimetre cannon, would you fire proportionately with the same type of weapon and the same number of shells?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Madam, they didn't have 130-millimetre cannons down there in the city. It has to be told that they didn't, so we didn't retaliate with that. We didn't retaliate with that kind of hardware.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. That's just an example, but the point I'm making - and I want to make sure I understand what you're saying in your statement - when you say proportionate fire, and you gave me an example of them firing two or three shells and you firing back I think you said first one shell and then you would follow-up, when you say "proportionate," are you talking about the number of shells or the type of weapon or both?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: One or perhaps two in order to stop them, in order to stop their fire. That's what I meant when I said "proportionate." It was our way of preventing them. We would fire one or two shells to that location, either to drive them away or simply to stop their fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you speak about this in paragraph 16 and you indicate just before this you took measures to reduce collateral civilian casualties, it is this proportionate analysis you're talking about that you applied, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Usually we would retaliate with one or two shells; however, there were also cases that, for example, from the military barracks, from the military hospital, or from the Kosevo Hospital that they opened fire from 120-millimetre hardware. We did not retaliate in those cases because we knew what kind of facilities those were and that also includes the military hospitals in Marin Dvor and Kosevo. We did not retaliate against those because we were always afraid of inflicting major civilian casualties if we had done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you have never fired at a hospital in Sarajevo, that your -- the 1st Sarajevo Militarised Brigade never fired at a hospital?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: That's correct and the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were there other targets -- or, excuse me, locations in this city that you would consider completely off limits?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar you are with Sarajevo. 99 per cent of the population around Sarajevo were Serbs and there were five UNPROFOR teams who supervised every firing position, the positions where the hardware was grouped and they monitored whether fire was opened from there. I can't tell you what was in Hrsaj [phoen], Brajlovici [phoen] or Ilidza. I can also talk about my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we can go to paragraph 18 of your statement which talks about specific areas. In paragraph 18 you said: "Of the military targets in the city under Muslim control I will list the following military targets in civilian areas ..." And then you list several places, Velesici, Ciglane, Bjelave, City Hall, Dobrinja, and Bistrik, and I want to now speak about those in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, could you leave five minutes at the end of today's session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P5926, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is a map of Sarajevo that contains all six of those locations. And, sir, in front of you, you have a booklet, as everyone does which for the record is 65 ter 23918 and if we can turn to that, it's on the desk in front of you. You'll also see it on the screen. And we'll have page 1 of this. Sir, directly in front of you on the desk underneath that map, take that off, there's a binder and I want you to -- yes, I want you to look directly at that. This reflects five of the areas that you spoke about in paragraph 18. We see Velesici, Ciglane, Bjelave, the down-town area and Bistrik. And then if you turn to page 2 you mentioned a sixth place, and that will be Dobrinja. Do these all look accurately placed for you? Does this look like an accurate representation of where they were located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: I don't see any of their firing positions anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you won't. This is solely a map. So we're going to go to page 3 of this map, and this is a blow-up of Velesici. And then if you go to -- and so what we're on is 65 ter 23918 and we're on page 3, but I think everybody in the courtroom probably has it. Page 3 is Velesici and, actually, if you can just turn quickly to page 4, it's a satellite image of Velesici. Mr. Skrba, could you describe the general nature of the area of Velesici? Was it industrial? Was it residential?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Velesici is a residential area with family houses and apartments. In the northern part there is a small industrial area in the direction of the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were there also schools in the area as well to support the residents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Most probably. I can't remember there were, but I believe that there were elementary schools there. I can't remember where they were, whether there were any and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you mentioned a tank from Velesici. I think you now have it up on the screen in front of us. Can you mark on the screen where the tank was located.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to get my bearings, although I'm a good topographer. It was somewhere above the tobacco factory, somewhere in that region, but I can't see the tobacco factory marked here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrba, as we continue I'm going to ask you for the locations of all the things that you mentioned in paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, may I make the suggestion that we pause here, Mr. Skrba can take this with him, he can take a look at it, and we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. Thank you, Ms. West. Very well. Mr. Skrba, we'll continue tomorrow and can I remind you that during the course of your testimony you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness can be excused. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're continuing on Monday; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just, I didn't want the witness to think he was needed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's very kind. Mr. Skrba -- okay. Did I say "tomorrow"?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies, I said "tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not be sitting tomorrow. We'll continue on Monday morning. I hope you have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, going back to your statement about your potential reply to the Prosecution's response in respect to protective measures, although I just said I noted your response -- your statement, there are a couple of points that I find it difficult to follow. First, take -- please don't take it for granted that the Chamber will allow your reply every time, but at the time when I heard your statement I thought that there are -- there were new information in the Prosecution's responses, but I'm not sure that was the situation. The -- first of all, you should obtain all the information you -- when you filed the motion firsthand, and then unless there's new information that warrants your further reply then you can contact the witnesses and file further information. But that should not be the practice, model practice, every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We understand that and we will endeavour and have endeavoured to get all the information from the witness at the beginning, but the Prosecution's responses have generally been that more information is required and the motion should be denied because inadequate information has been provided. And so we want to give the witness the opportunity to see if there's anything that they -- now hearing from the Prosecution that they would like us to tell the Chamber. We think that this is an important part of the process for witnesses, because if you do deny the protective measures, as you've done every time so far, we want them to have the opportunity or at least the feeling that they got to say everything that they wanted to say before such a decision was taken. And particularly in some cases where we don't support the protective measures, we think it's important that the witness's situation be fully conveyed to the Chamber. So that's -- you see we filed very, very infrequent replies before this Chamber, but in this particular case, while we will endeavour to get all the information in advance, we feel it's important that the witness be given a full opportunity to bring anything that they think is important to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's exactly the situation I was concerned about. You can expect the Prosecution's response to the effect that your motion was not supported with sufficient material, or et cetera. You should prepare everything at the beginning -- in the beginning. Please bear that in mind. Very well. The hearing will be adjourned for the week and will resume next week on Monday. Thank you.
